newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines readies for 1998 political fiesta.
newsitem.headline: Philippines readies for 1998 political fiesta.

text.p: With nearly a year and a half before the Philippines holds its next presidential elections, signs have emerged of a heated but fiesta-like battle ahead, political analysts said on Sunday.

Although President Fidel Ramos holds office until June 1998, newspapers are already bandying more than a dozen names as potential presidential aspirants, ranging from a former movie actor with massive popular appeal to a fiery former female judge who once challenged Ramos to a fist fight.

Since Ferdinand Marcos was ousted in 1986 from the presidency after 20 years in office, which included 14 years of martial law, the Philippines has become one of Asia's most free-wheeling democracies.

Analysts said they expect speculation on potential candidates to dominate most of 1997. Once the campaign begins early next year, they expect a replay of 1992 polls when candidates sang, danced and enlisted the support of movie and television stars to win votes.
"Politics is our number one industry, it brings up a fiesta atmosphere, takes our mind off our problems," political analyst Teodoro Benigno said.
"We have much a longer tradition in electoral politics than most nations," said Alex Magno, a political science professor at the University of the Philippines.
"In our political tradition, it's always winner take all and the presidency is the most important plum. Whoever gets the presidency, gets everything."
Ramos, who many analysts regard as one of the country's most popular leaders ever, is barred by the constitution from seeking another term.
A move to amend the constitution to allow him to seek re-election seems to have dwindled because of his recent health problems, analysts said.

Ramos, 68, underwent major surgery two weeks ago to remove a life-threatening cholesterol blockage in a vein on his neck which had impeded flow of blood to the brain. Doctors said the blockage could have induced a massive stroke.
"He (Ramos) will be a tough act to follow," industrialist Raul Concepcion said, referring to the former army general's success in office.
Ramos is credited with pioneering a reforms programme which has turned the nation's hobbled economy into one of the fastest growing in Asia.
Nevertheless, opposition parties are exploring possible alliances to match the administration's political machine.
Within the president's Lakas (People's Power) party, aspirants are vying for Ramos's personal endorsement, seen as crucial to victory at the polls.
Analysts predict the current broad field of aspirants will narrow down to anywhere from three to six candidates by the official beginning of the campaign period in March next year.
The short list is likely to include:

- Vice-President Joseph Estrada, an ex-actor who specialised in "tough guy" roles fighting for the oppressed. He enjoys huge support among the poorer classes and has not lost an election since he entered politics to run as a town mayor in 1972.

- Opposition senator Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, an economist. A daughter of former Philippine president Diosdado Macapagal, she and Estrada have topped popularity surveys among potential presidential candidates.

- Miriam Santiago, a feisty former judge who vows to jail all corrupt officials if she becomes president. She narrowly lost to Ramos in a seven-sided presidential race in 1992, accused him of poll fraud and challenged him to a boxing match. Ramos did not take up the offer.
- Defence Secretary Renato de Villa, a staunch Ramos loyalist. Newspapers have speculated recently that Ramos is considering endorsing his long-time military ally as his presidential choice.
- House of Representatives Speaker Jose de Venecia, a close presidential confidant. He has fared poorly in survey ratings but counts on the support of many congressmen.
- Opposition senator Edgardo Angara. He is president of the main opposition LDP (Filipino Democratic Struggle) but, like de Venecia, is lowly rated in opinion polls.
